Hero Law and Quirk Use.text: In Japan, using a Quirk in public is legal only in narrow cases. Licensed heroes may use their Quirks on duty. Everyone else may use a Quirk in private, at work where the job and its permits allow it, and in supervised training at a school or licensed facility. Small, harmless everyday uses in public are tolerated in practice, but anything that could injure someone or damage property counts as misuse. Using a Quirk against another person is the line the law cares about most. A civilian who attacks with a Quirk is a criminal, and the press and the police call that person a villain whatever the motive. Self-defense is the main exception: a person may use a Quirk to escape an immediate attack, with only the force needed. Stepping in to save someone else is a gray zone. Police and courts weigh how urgent the danger was, whether a hero or officer was present and how much force and damage followed; the usual result is a statement and a warning, sometimes a fine, and a charge when someone gets hurt. Fighting a villain without a license, chasing a suspect or patrolling as a vigilante is illegal even when it ends well. Penalties run from warnings and fines to arrest, prison and a criminal record that can bar a person from ever holding a hero license. Hero students are bound by the same laws: on campus and under a teacher's supervision they may train freely, but off campus they have no more authority than any other citizen until they earn a provisional license.
